title: Files
overview: Variables live in main memory and vanish when a program stops, so anything that must survive to the next run, be shared with another program or be too large to type in again belongs in a file. At AS level the files are text files: a series of lines, each ended by an end-of-line marker, with an end-of-file marker after the last line. Paper 2 expects fluent Cambridge pseudocode for them: OPENFILE <name> FOR READ, WRITE or APPEND, READFILE and WRITEFILE one line at a time, an EOF() check to drive a loop over a file of unknown length, and CLOSEFILE when finished. Marks are lost for choosing WRITE (which wipes the file) when APPEND was needed, for reading with a fixed-count loop or a single IF, for doing arithmetic on a line without STR_TO_NUM, and for forgetting to close the file.
syllabusPoints: Show understanding of why files are needed, including keeping data permanently between program runs and passing data between programs.
Write pseudocode to handle text files that consist of one or more lines, using OPENFILE <filename> FOR READ / WRITE / APPEND, READFILE, WRITEFILE, EOF() and CLOSEFILE.

definitions.definition: A named block of data kept on secondary storage. It stays there after the program that created it has finished, unlike the contents of variables in RAM.
A file holding characters arranged as lines. Every line finishes with an end-of-line marker, and an end-of-file marker follows the final line. Every value read from it arrives as a string.
Makes a file available to the program in one stated mode: OPENFILE <filename> FOR READ, FOR WRITE or FOR APPEND. No READFILE or WRITEFILE is allowed on a file until it has been opened.
READFILE <filename>, <variable> copies the next unread line of a file opened FOR READ into a STRING variable and moves the read position on by one line.
WRITEFILE <filename>, <string> adds one new line to a file opened FOR WRITE or FOR APPEND.
Starts the file empty: a missing file is created, and an existing file loses everything it held. New lines are written from the start.
Keeps every existing line and places each new line after the last one already in the file.
EOF(<filename>) is a BOOLEAN function that returns TRUE when no unread lines remain in a file opened FOR READ (including when the file is empty) and FALSE otherwise.
CLOSEFILE <filename> ends the program's use of a file. It releases the file for other programs and makes sure buffered lines are actually saved to storage.

sections.title: Why files are needed
content: Everything a running program holds, whether a single counter or a large array, sits in main memory (RAM). When the program ends, or the computer is switched off, that memory is released and the values are gone. A file is saved on secondary storage such as an SSD or hard disk, so its contents are still there next time. A program can save its data to a file before it stops and load it back at the start of the following run.

Persistence is the main reason, but not the only one. A file can be opened by a different program, sent to another computer or read by a person in a text editor, so it is a common way to pass data between programs and users. Files let a program process far more data than could be typed in at the keyboard each time, and they can hold more than fits in memory at once, because the program reads one line at a time. They are also used to keep a lasting record of output, such as a log, a report or a backup copy.
bullets: Variables are held in RAM and are lost when the program terminates; a file on secondary storage survives between runs.
Data saved in a file can be reloaded later instead of being entered again by the user.
Files let data be exchanged between different programs, users and computers.
Large data sets can be kept in a file and processed one line at a time.
Output such as logs, reports and backups can be stored for later use.

sections.title: What a text file looks like
content: At AS level every file is a text file. It is simply a series of characters divided into lines. After each line the file stores an invisible end-of-line marker, and after the final line it stores an end-of-file marker. You can make or inspect a text file in any plain text editor, which is a handy way to prepare test data for a program.

Because a text file holds only characters, it has no idea what type a value was meant to be. A line such as 64 is stored as the characters 6 and 4. When it is read back with READFILE it arrives as the STRING "64". In the same way, WRITEFILE expects a string, so a number is normally turned into text with NUM_TO_STR before it is written. One line usually holds one data item or one record.
bullets: A text file is a sequence of lines; each line ends with an end-of-line marker and the file ends with an end-of-file marker.
READFILE and WRITEFILE work on one whole line at a time.
Every line read is a STRING; use STR_TO_NUM to turn it into a number and NUM_TO_STR to turn a number into a string for writing.

examples.label: The file Marks.txt used in the examples below
examples.content:
Marks.txt (one mark per line)
line 1: 64
line 2: 38
line 3: 81
line 4: 50
line 5: 47
(end-of-file marker)

Each line is stored as characters, so READFILE returns "64", "38", ... as strings.

sections.title: The file-handling statements and the open-use-close pattern
content: Cambridge pseudocode has a small, fixed set of file statements. OPENFILE <filename> FOR <mode> prepares a file for one kind of use: READ, WRITE or APPEND. READFILE <filename>, <variable> takes the next line from a file opened for reading. WRITEFILE <filename>, <string> puts a line into a file opened for writing or appending. EOF(<filename>) reports whether any lines remain to be read. CLOSEFILE <filename> ends the use of the file.

Every file task follows the same outline: open in the right mode, carry out the reads or writes, then close. The mode decides which statements are legal. You cannot WRITEFILE to a file opened FOR READ or READFILE from a file opened FOR WRITE or APPEND. If a program needs to read a file and then add to it, it closes the file and opens it again in the second mode. The filename can be a string literal such as "Marks.txt" or a STRING variable that holds the name.
bullets: Order is always OPENFILE, then READFILE/WRITEFILE, then CLOSEFILE.
FOR READ allows READFILE and EOF(); FOR WRITE and FOR APPEND allow WRITEFILE.
To switch mode, close the file and open it again in the new mode.

examples.label: Syntax summary of the file statements
examples.content:
OPENFILE <filename> FOR READ      // existing file, read only
READFILE <filename>, <variable>   // next line into a STRING variable
EOF(<filename>)                   // TRUE when no lines are left

OPENFILE <filename> FOR WRITE     // new or emptied file
OPENFILE <filename> FOR APPEND    // keep contents, add to the end
WRITEFILE <filename>, <string>    // write one line

CLOSEFILE <filename>              // finish with the file

sections.title: Why a file must be closed
content: While a program has a file open, the operating system may stop other programs from using it. Closing the file removes that restriction. Writing is also buffered: lines passed to WRITEFILE are collected in memory and copied to the disk in blocks, because that is faster than one disk operation per line. CLOSEFILE forces anything still in the buffer to be saved. A program that writes a file but never closes it may leave the last lines, or all of them, unsaved.

Closing also resets the file so it can be opened again in another mode later in the same program. As a habit, write the CLOSEFILE statement straight after writing the OPENFILE, then fill in the processing between them.
bullets: CLOSEFILE releases the file so other programs and processes can use it.
CLOSEFILE flushes the write buffer, so data written is really stored.
Every OPENFILE needs a matching CLOSEFILE once processing of that file is complete.

sections.title: Writing a text file
content: Writing usually means creating a file from scratch. OPENFILE <filename> FOR WRITE makes a new empty file, or empties an existing one. Each WRITEFILE then adds one line after the previous one. A common task is saving the contents of an array so they can be reloaded in a later run: loop through the array and write one element per line.

WRITEFILE takes a string. If the data is numeric, convert it with NUM_TO_STR first. For a record with several fields, the fields can be joined into one line with a separator such as a comma, using the & concatenation operator.
bullets: Open FOR WRITE, write one line per WRITEFILE, then CLOSEFILE.
Opening FOR WRITE erases any old contents before the first line is written.
Convert numbers with NUM_TO_STR, and join record fields with & and a separator, before writing.

examples.label: Worked example: saving an array of names to Members.txt
examples.content:
DECLARE Names : ARRAY[1:3] OF STRING
DECLARE Index : INTEGER

Names[1] ← "Priya"
Names[2] ← "Tomas"
Names[3] ← "Keiko"

OPENFILE "Members.txt" FOR WRITE
FOR Index ← 1 TO 3
   WRITEFILE "Members.txt", Names[Index]
NEXT Index
CLOSEFILE "Members.txt"

Members.txt afterwards (whatever it held before is gone):
line 1: Priya
line 2: Tomas
line 3: Keiko

sections.title: Reading a text file line by line
content: Reading needs a file that already exists. After OPENFILE <filename> FOR READ, the read position is at the first line. Each READFILE copies the current line into a STRING variable and moves the position down one line, so successive READFILE statements return the lines in order from top to bottom. There is no way to go back to an earlier line except to close the file and open it again.

If the exact number of lines is known, for example a settings file that always has two lines, the program can simply call READFILE that many times. Most files, however, have a length that is not known in advance, and that needs the EOF() loop shown later.
bullets: FOR READ needs an existing file; the read position starts at line 1.
Each READFILE returns the next line and advances the position; reading is strictly sequential.
A fixed number of READFILE calls is only safe when the number of lines is guaranteed.

examples.label: Worked example: reading the first two lines of Members.txt
examples.content:
DECLARE First, Second : STRING

OPENFILE "Members.txt" FOR READ
READFILE "Members.txt", First
READFILE "Members.txt", Second
CLOSEFILE "Members.txt"
OUTPUT First, " and ", Second

Members.txt holds: Priya / Tomas / Keiko
Output:
Priya and Tomas
(Keiko is never read.)

sections.title: WRITE versus APPEND
content: Both modes allow WRITEFILE, but they treat existing contents in opposite ways. FOR WRITE throws away the old contents as soon as the file is opened, even if the program then writes nothing. FOR APPEND keeps every line and places new lines after the last one. If the file does not exist yet, both modes create it.

The choice follows from the task. Use WRITE when the file should hold only the new data, for example saving the full current state of an array, which replaces the last save. Use APPEND when data builds up over time and earlier lines must be kept, for example adding each new sale to a sales log or each new member to a membership list.
bullets: WRITE: file emptied (or created), then new lines written from the top.
APPEND: existing lines kept, new lines added at the end (file created if missing).
Opening FOR WRITE by mistake destroys earlier data and cannot be undone by the program.

examples.label: Worked example: APPEND then WRITE on Members.txt

sections.title: Reading a whole file with WHILE NOT EOF()
content: To process every line of a file of unknown length, test EOF() before each read. EOF(<filename>) returns FALSE while there is still at least one unread line and TRUE once the last line has been read. The loop WHILE NOT EOF(<filename>) therefore runs exactly once per line and stops by itself, whether the file has three lines or three thousand.

A pre-condition WHILE loop is the right choice because the test happens before the first READFILE. If the file is empty, EOF() is TRUE straight away and the loop body never runs. A REPEAT ... UNTIL EOF() loop would work for a file with at least one line, but on an empty file it would try to read a line that does not exist. To load a file into an array, keep a separate index that goes up by one after each line, and stop if the array becomes full.
bullets: Pattern: OPENFILE ... FOR READ, WHILE NOT EOF(file), READFILE, process, ENDWHILE, CLOSEFILE.
WHILE tests before reading, so an empty file is handled safely; REPEAT ... UNTIL does not.
Do not use a FOR loop with a guessed count, or a single IF, to read a file of unknown length.

examples.label: Worked example: numbering and counting every line of Marks.txt
examples.content:
DECLARE LineData : STRING
DECLARE LineCount : INTEGER

LineCount ← 0
OPENFILE "Marks.txt" FOR READ
WHILE NOT EOF("Marks.txt")
   READFILE "Marks.txt", LineData
   LineCount ← LineCount + 1
   OUTPUT LineCount, ": ", LineData
ENDWHILE
CLOSEFILE "Marks.txt"
OUTPUT "Lines read: ", LineCount

Marks.txt holds: 64 / 38 / 81 / 50 / 47

EOF before read | LineData | LineCount
FALSE           | "64"     | 1
FALSE           | "38"     | 2
FALSE           | "81"     | 3
FALSE           | "50"     | 4
FALSE           | "47"     | 5
TRUE            | loop ends

Output:
1: 64
2: 38
3: 81
4: 50
5: 47
Lines read: 5

If Marks.txt were empty, EOF is TRUE at the first test, the loop body never runs, and the only output is: Lines read: 0

examples.label: Loading a file into an array without overrunning it
examples.content:
DECLARE Marks : ARRAY[1:30] OF STRING
DECLARE Index : INTEGER

Index ← 0
OPENFILE "Marks.txt" FOR READ
WHILE NOT EOF("Marks.txt") AND Index < 30
   Index ← Index + 1
   READFILE "Marks.txt", Marks[Index]
ENDWHILE
CLOSEFILE "Marks.txt"
// With the five-line Marks.txt: Marks[1..5] = "64","38","81","50","47" and Index = 5

sections.title: Converting what is read before calculating
content: READFILE always places a string in its variable. Before a line can be added, averaged or compared as a number it must be converted with STR_TO_NUM. Without the conversion, an attempt to add the string to an INTEGER is a type error. In languages where + also joins strings, the values are glued together as text instead of added, which gives a result that looks like a number but is wrong.

Note that INT() is not the right function here: in Cambridge pseudocode INT(x) takes a REAL and returns its whole-number part. STR_TO_NUM(x) is the function that turns a numeric string into a number. Going the other way, NUM_TO_STR(x) prepares a number for WRITEFILE.
bullets: Every line read is a STRING, whatever it looks like.
Use STR_TO_NUM(LineData) before arithmetic or numeric comparison; use NUM_TO_STR before writing a number.
Adding unconverted strings either fails or concatenates them.

examples.label: Worked example: total and average of Marks.txt
examples.content:
DECLARE LineData : STRING
DECLARE Total, Count : INTEGER

Total ← 0
Count ← 0
OPENFILE "Marks.txt" FOR READ
WHILE NOT EOF("Marks.txt")
   READFILE "Marks.txt", LineData
   Total ← Total + STR_TO_NUM(LineData)
   Count ← Count + 1
ENDWHILE
CLOSEFILE "Marks.txt"
IF Count > 0 THEN
   OUTPUT "Total: ", Total, " Average: ", Total / Count
ENDIF

Total: 64 + 38 + 81 + 50 + 47 = 280, Count = 5
Output (/ always gives a REAL):
Total: 280 Average: 56.0

Without STR_TO_NUM, joining the strings would give "6438815047" instead of 280.

sections.title: Copying and filtering one file into another
content: Many exam tasks combine reading and writing: read each line of a source file and write some or all of the lines to a second file. Both files are open at once, one FOR READ and the other FOR WRITE (or APPEND if the target should keep what it already holds). A straight copy writes every line it reads. A filter tests each line and writes only those that meet a condition, converting with STR_TO_NUM first if the test is numeric.

Because WRITEFILE takes a string, a line that was read and not changed can be written back exactly as it was, with no conversion. A program can only change a text file by writing a new version, so updating one line of a file also follows this pattern: copy every line into a new file, writing the changed line in place of the old one.
bullets: Open the source FOR READ and the target FOR WRITE or APPEND; close both at the end.
Loop WHILE NOT EOF(source), test each line, and WRITEFILE the lines that pass.
Editing one line of a text file means writing a new copy of the file with that line replaced.

examples.label: Worked example: copying marks of 50 or more into Passed.txt
examples.content:
DECLARE LineData : STRING
DECLARE Copied : INTEGER

Copied ← 0
OPENFILE "Marks.txt" FOR READ
OPENFILE "Passed.txt" FOR WRITE
WHILE NOT EOF("Marks.txt")
   READFILE "Marks.txt", LineData
   IF STR_TO_NUM(LineData) >= 50 THEN
      WRITEFILE "Passed.txt", LineData
      Copied ← Copied + 1
   ENDIF
ENDWHILE
CLOSEFILE "Marks.txt"
CLOSEFILE "Passed.txt"
OUTPUT Copied, " marks copied"

LineData | >= 50? | Written | Copied
"64"     | TRUE   | 64      | 1
"38"     | FALSE  | -       | 1
"81"     | TRUE   | 81      | 2
"50"     | TRUE   | 50      | 3
"47"     | FALSE  | -       | 3

Passed.txt afterwards: 64 / 81 / 50
Output:
3 marks copied

analysisChains.title: Why an IF reads only one line
steps: Marks.txt holds five lines and a program must output all of them
The program uses IF NOT EOF("Marks.txt") THEN READFILE ... OUTPUT ... ENDIF
The IF is executed once, so only line 1 (64) is read and output
Nothing sends control back to test EOF again, so lines 2 to 5 are ignored
analysisChains.evaluation: Repetition is needed, not selection: replacing IF ... ENDIF with WHILE NOT EOF("Marks.txt") ... ENDWHILE makes the read-and-output steps run once for each of the five lines and stop at the end of the file.

analysisChains.title: Why WRITE lost a year of records
steps: Sales.txt already holds 200 lines from earlier runs
Today's program must add 3 new sales
It opens the file with OPENFILE "Sales.txt" FOR WRITE and writes the 3 lines
Opening FOR WRITE empties the file before the first WRITEFILE, so the 200 old lines are gone
analysisChains.evaluation: The file ends up with 3 lines instead of 203. The task needs existing data kept, so the correct mode is FOR APPEND, which leaves the 200 lines in place and writes the 3 new sales after them.

analysisChains.title: Why the total came out as a long string of digits
steps: A program reads Marks.txt (64, 38, 81, 50, 47) and adds each LineData to Total
LineData is a STRING because READFILE always returns text
In a language where + joins strings, Total becomes "6438815047"; in a strictly typed one the addition is rejected
Neither result is the intended numeric total
analysisChains.evaluation: Each line must be converted before arithmetic: Total ← Total + STR_TO_NUM(LineData) gives 280, and dividing by the 5 lines read gives an average of 56.

examTips: Write file statements exactly: OPENFILE "X.txt" FOR READ, READFILE "X.txt", Var, WRITEFILE "X.txt", Value, EOF("X.txt"), CLOSEFILE "X.txt". Each is often a separate mark.
When the number of lines is not given, read with WHILE NOT EOF(...) ... ENDWHILE, testing before each READFILE.
Read the question for the words 'add to' or 'keep existing data' (APPEND) versus 'create' or 'replace' (WRITE).
Convert with STR_TO_NUM before any calculation or numeric comparison on a line read from a file.
Close every file you open, and close both files in a copy or filter algorithm.
commonMistakes: Using IF NOT EOF(...) instead of WHILE NOT EOF(...), so only one line is processed.
Opening FOR WRITE when the task says add to the file, erasing the existing contents.
Using a REPEAT ... UNTIL EOF() loop that tries to read from an empty file.
Doing arithmetic on the STRING from READFILE instead of converting with STR_TO_NUM.
Using READFILE on a file opened FOR WRITE or APPEND, or WRITEFILE on a file opened FOR READ.
Leaving out CLOSEFILE, or closing the file inside the loop after the first line.

quickRecall.question: Give three reasons why files are needed.
quickRecall.answer: Data in variables is lost when the program ends, so a file keeps it between runs; files let data be passed between programs, users and computers; files hold large data sets and lasting output such as logs and backups.

quickRecall.question: Describe the structure of a text file.
quickRecall.answer: A sequence of lines of characters; each line ends with an end-of-line marker and the file ends with an end-of-file marker.

quickRecall.question: Write the statement to open Log.txt so new lines go after the existing ones.
What happens to an existing file opened FOR WRITE?
quickRecall.answer: Its contents are erased when it is opened, and new lines are written from the start.

quickRecall.question: What does EOF("Data.txt") return and why is it tested before READFILE?
quickRecall.answer: TRUE when no unread lines remain, otherwise FALSE. Testing first means an empty file is handled and the program never reads past the last line.

quickRecall.question: Why is STR_TO_NUM needed after READFILE?
quickRecall.answer: READFILE always returns a STRING, so the value must be converted to a number before it can be used in arithmetic or numeric comparison.

quickRecall.question: Give two reasons for CLOSEFILE.
quickRecall.answer: It releases the file for other programs, and it makes sure any buffered lines are actually written to storage.

quickRecall.question: How do you keep only the lines of A.txt that meet a condition in B.txt?
quickRecall.answer: Open A.txt FOR READ and B.txt FOR WRITE, loop WHILE NOT EOF("A.txt") reading each line, WRITEFILE it to B.txt if it meets the condition, then close both files.
